negative_results: Past-oriented language showed no stable separation: mean user-normalized post share was 7.2% for diagnosed users versus 7.3% for controls, with mixed fold directions.
Certainty markers were essentially null (2.4% versus 2.4% of posts); the modest increase in hedging should not be interpreted as globally reduced certainty.
Generic social-connectedness vocabulary was nearly identical (14.4% versus 14.1%), so mentions of friends or family alone are weak evidence.
Raw post-weighted rates can reverse user-level results: direct-mention posts were 38.3% of diagnosed posts versus 42.2% of control posts, while mean within-user shares were 34.8% versus 32.8%.
Positive affect was not lower among diagnosed users; it was higher as well (14.1% versus 12.5% of posts), so negative affect is not a unipolar mood measure.
Quoted or lyric-like material was common and stylistically variable; lyric cues were slightly higher among diagnosed users, while quote punctuation was slightly higher among controls.
First-person singular prevalence alone saturated near ceiling, making raw pronoun counts substantially less useful than normalized rates, context, and persistence.
